column3: Pairs kindness to near kin and needy people with the focus's restored support network.
Frames a response to injury beside God's pardoning and forgiving character.
Names divine bounty, but gives no direction on retaining aid after harm.
Urges spending in God's path, supporting the focus's refusal to close a generous outlet.
Sets the surah's binding framework, without adding to pardon or continued provision.
Explicitly commands pardon and overlooking after repeated betrayal, closely matching the focus's response to injury.
Requires provision and gracious speech for kin and needy people at distribution.
Addresses marital eligibility, not forgiveness or continuing material support.
Counsels contentment with God's bounty, only loosely related to giving from abundance.
Defines righteousness through giving loved wealth to kin and needy people.
Unites spending, restraining anger, and pardoning others in one ethic of excellence.
Calls a harmful utterance false while naming God pardoning and forgiving.
Directs shared resources to kin and needy people so wealth does not remain among the rich.
Provides the legal backdrop to the accusation passage but not its call to forgive.
Condemns withholding God's bounty and encouraging others to withhold, opposing the focus's closed-off aid.
Commends waiving one's due and not forgetting bounty between people.
Recalls God's grace amid the circulated report that caused the focus's injury.
After warning of intimate hostility, commands pardon, overlooking, and forgiveness.
Links love of God with receiving forgiveness, without a social act of pardon.
Mentions the clear Book without a relevant relation to aid or forgiveness.
Only states that the event is seen as near.
Keeps kinship and emigrant bonds in view and permits doing recognized good to allies.
Supplies the sanction for unproven accusations that forms the surrounding cause of injury.
States that bounty is in God's hand, without directing its social use.
Values spending wealth in God's path, relevant to sustaining those committed to that path.
Continues the passage's regulated treatment of accusations, clarifying the injury's setting.
Commands giving the due of kin and needy people for God's sake.
Names the emigrants and God's merciful turning toward them in hardship.
Reiterates that divine bounty is granted by God, but not how it is shared.
Commands a beautiful overlooking, a direct complement to the focus's pardon.
Combines giving, service in God's path, and seeking God's forgiveness.
Opens forgiveness to those who repent and repair after the slander-related offense.
Counters fear of poverty with God's promise of forgiveness and bounty, supporting continued giving.
Includes goodness to kin and needy people, though earlier cards give the closer provision formulation.
Warns disbelievers of their final destination without bearing on the focus.
Mentions God's abundance after separation, only broadly echoing material capacity.
Models releasing blame after grave personal injury while invoking God's forgiveness.
Defines the Messenger's duty of conveyance, not aid or pardon.
Seeks God's pardon, forgiveness, and mercy, grounding the focus's appeal to be forgiven.
Names later believers who emigrated and kinship priority, but not their support.
Continues the accusation procedure, with only contextual value after the earlier cards.
States God's freedom to forgive and His merciful character.
Names emigrants in God's path and divine forgiveness, connecting two focus terms.
Directly precedes the focus: believers should have assumed good and rejected the slander.
Names God's pardoning and forgiving character without a relational response.
Mentions divine bounty alone.
Shows pardon limiting harmful disclosure, a distant parallel to not perpetuating injury.
Calls for grateful use of provision but gives no relevant interpersonal instruction.
Denies forgiveness to those dying in disbelief, outside the focus's concern.
Continues the oath procedure surrounding accusations, but adds little beyond earlier context.
Commands prostration and nearness without a link to the focus.
Records God's pardon after communal disobedience and names His favor toward believers.
Commands obedience to divine judgment, only generally related to the surah's norms.
Sets a boundary on seeking forgiveness even for near kin, qualifying the focus's broad appeal to forgiveness.
Addresses marriage to believing bondwomen and its legal conditions.
Refers to an earlier people's questions and disbelief.
Shows confession of wrong and immediate appeal to God's forgiveness.
Describes a messenger's departure after delivering counsel.
Completes the oath procedure without adding to the focus's pardon or support.
Describes creation and God's mastery of the heavenly bodies.
Makes spending what one loves a condition of righteousness, strengthening costly generosity.
Regulates entering uninhabited houses.
Forbids exalting oneself against God.
Names God's forgiveness after a marital oath, only a remote relational parallel.
Commands giving kin and needy people their due, though this repeats the earlier direct distribution theme.
Directs warning to the nearest clan, naming kin without a duty of provision.
Rebukes love of the immediate world.
Invokes God's grace, mercy, and acceptance of repentance in the same passage.
Calls for uprightness and seeking forgiveness, without the focus's interpersonal repair.
Commands pardon and overlooking in the face of hostile envy, reinforcing nonretaliation.
Addresses dress permission for elderly women.
Names God as worthy of reverence and forgiveness.
Expresses hope for forgiveness on the Day of Judgment.
Condemns waste, preserving the resource-flow side of the focus's generosity.
Names God as forgiving and loving, without a human act of pardon.
Contrasts people of means who avoid effort in God's path with the focus's open-handed use of means.
Begins the false-accusation account whose harm the focus answers with restored generosity.
Describes division after clear evidence arrived.
Praises wisdom without a specific connection to aid or forgiveness.
Condemns those who want indecency spread among believers, directly framing the offense behind the focus.
Affirms that the messengers brought truth.
Commends following the best of what is heard, without a specific relation to pardon or support.
Joins gentleness, pardoning others, and seeking forgiveness for them after collective failure.
States that God overlooks much after affliction, supporting mercy beyond strict retribution.
Promises divine forgiveness to those who answer God's caller.
Depicts the futility of disbelievers' deeds.
Recalls God's pardon after wrongdoing, but without the focus's social repair.
Contains a warning of impending woe.
Promises believers their reward and describes God as forgiving and merciful.
Exposes people who would withhold even the smallest share, a contrast to open-handed giving.
Contrasts false assumptions about God with truth, only distantly related to the focus's moral response.
A prayer for divine forgiveness without an interpersonal counterpart.
Regulates sacred months and conflict with idolaters.
Commands seeking forgiveness for believing men and women, echoing the focus's desire for God's forgiveness.
Announces condemnation of disbelievers.
Reports knowledge granted to David and Solomon and their gratitude.
Announces the Messenger's arrival after a gap between messengers.
Expresses hope for forgiveness after becoming first believers.
States that the brought-near witness the record.
Describes receiving one's record in the right hand.
Directs spending toward parents, near kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers.
Identifies surplus as what should be given, supporting generosity from material capacity.
Protects charitable giving from reminders and injury, directly opposing aid made conditional by resentment.
Makes kind speech and forgiveness better than charity followed by injury.
Warns that reminders and injury can nullify charity, clarifying why support must remain free of retaliation.
Commands spending from good earnings and produce rather than withholding the worthy share.
Commends alms given to poor people, especially when concealed.
Identifies needy people constrained in God's path as deserving recipients of provision.
Calls remission of a debt to a person in hardship better than insisting on repayment.
Calls believers to forgiveness from their Lord, echoing the focus's appeal to seek divine forgiveness.
Links acknowledged wrongdoing with seeking God's forgiveness.
Affirms an assigned share for near kin in inherited wealth, reinforcing kinship as a route for provision.
Urges care for vulnerable descendants and speaking rightly, joining material responsibility with humane speech.
Makes charity, recognized good, and reconciliation the valuable exceptions to private conversation.
Pairs pardoning a wrong with God's pardoning power, closely matching the focus's final appeal.
Forbids hatred from diverting people from justice, constraining the response to injury.
Names pardon as expiation after injury, providing a direct alternative to equal retaliation.
Requires feeding or clothing needy people as expiation for broken oaths.
Promises mercy and forgiveness to those who do wrong then repair.
Seeks God's forgiveness and mercy after communal wrongdoing.
Commands accepting pardon, enjoining recognized good, and turning away from ignorance.
Names believers who emigrated, gave refuge, and gave aid, directly supporting care for emigrants.
Again joins emigration with giving refuge and aid among believers.
Links emigration and striving with wealth in God's path.
Assigns charitable resources to poor and needy people and to causes in God's path.
Portrays people in hardship asking for charitable provision and affirms its reward.
Shows wrongdoers asking a close relative to seek forgiveness for them.
Answers that request with an intention to seek God's forgiveness for them.
Combines patient endurance, spending privately and openly, and repelling evil with good.
Commands excellence and giving to near kin as a foundational social duty.
Permits proportionate response to injury while presenting patient restraint as better.
Forbids keeping one's hand chained to the neck, a direct image against closing the outlet of provision.
Commands the best speech to prevent destructive discord among people.
Requires gentle speech even in confrontation with Pharaoh, a distant restraint on hostile response.
Includes giving from provision among the marks of devoted believers.
Promises a good provision to those who emigrated in God's path and were killed or died.
Commands repelling evil with what is best, a direct pattern for ending retaliatory escalation.
Recalls God's grace, mercy, and compassion in the same false-accusation passage.
Precedes the focus by warning against Satan and locating purification in God's grace and mercy.
Condemns accusing chaste, unsuspecting believing women, further defining the injury addressed by the focus.
Praises spending that is neither wasteful nor miserly, preserving a balanced generous flow.
Commends passing by falsehood with dignity, a restraint relevant to the circulating slander.
Promises to remove the evil of believers' deeds, a general divine-forgiveness parallel.
Commands engagement in the best manner, except with persistent wrongdoers.
Requires recognized companionship with parents despite grave disagreement, preserving relation without approval of harm.
Includes forgiveness among the rewarded qualities of believing women and men.
Forbids despair of God's mercy and declares His encompassing forgiveness.
Shows angels seeking forgiveness for believers and asking that mercy encompass them.
Commands repelling evil with what is better until hostility can become close friendship.
Names God as accepting repentance and pardoning evil deeds.
Praises those who forgive when angered.
Makes forgiveness and reconciliation a divinely rewarded response to injury.
Names patience and forgiveness as matters of steadfast resolve.
Commands turning away and saying peace in the face of rejection.
Directs believers to forgive those who do not expect God's days, withholding personal retaliation.
Commands reconciliation between fighting groups and justice if one persists in aggression.
Treats believers as siblings and commands reconciliation between them.
Forbids suspicion, spying, and backbiting, directly guarding against the social harm behind the focus.
Uses lending generously to God as an image for open-handed giving.
Promises multiplied return and generous reward to charitable men and women.
Identifies poor emigrants driven from their homes and property as recipients of support.
Praises those who prefer emigrant newcomers over themselves even when personally in need.
Permits kindness and justice toward those who do not fight or expel believers.
Commands spending from what one has while warning against the soul's own stinginess.
Pairs generous lending with multiplication and forgiveness from God.
Requires the person with abundance to spend from that abundance and others according to their means.
Describes believers' wealth as carrying a known due.
Identifies the petitioner and deprived person as recipients of that due.
Praises feeding needy people, orphans, and captives despite love for the food.
Frames that feeding as seeking God alone, without repayment or thanks.
Names an orphan among near kin as a priority in a time of hunger.
Names a needy person in destitution as a priority in a time of hunger.
Praises the one who gives wealth in pursuit of purification.
Forbids harsh treatment of the orphan.
Forbids repelling the petitioner, directly constraining refusal of need.
Commands speaking of the Lord's bounty, a distant counterpoint to concealing it.
Condemns driving away the orphan.
Condemns failure to urge feeding a needy person.
